lead: A single clever idea is not enough to build IoT. It works because several mature technologies arrived at low cost at the same time: cheap sensors and RFID tags to sense and identify, microcontrollers to compute locally, radio links to carry data, cellular networks to reach anywhere, cloud servers to store it, and analytics to make sense of it. Each technology was built for another purpose and then reused. A Bengaluru fleet tracker combines all of them: a GPS chip, a microcontroller, a SIM, a cloud dashboard and a fuel-wastage report. This chapter takes the technologies one at a time and shows the job each one does.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for the parts inside a device, and 1.5 for where each part sits in a layered architecture.

blocks.text: A sensor converts a physical quantity — temperature, motion, light — into an electrical signal. Cheap micro-machined sensors are the first reason IoT became practical: measurement turned into a component costing a few rupees instead of a laboratory instrument.

RFID supplies identity. A reader radiates a radio field; a passive tag harvests that energy, wakes up and returns the ID stored in its chip. No battery, no contact, no line of sight. The FASTag on an Indian car windscreen is an RFID tag read at a toll lane. RFID answers “which thing is this”, not “how hot is it”.

A wireless sensor network (WSN) is many small nodes, each with a sensor, a radio, a microcontroller and a battery. Radio range is short, so nodes forward each other's packets hop by hop until they reach a gateway. The hardware side is in Unit 2.

Embedded computing is the third piece. A microcontroller is one chip holding a CPU, flash program memory, RAM and input/output pins; it runs a single program forever, draws milliamps and costs tens of rupees. A single-board computer runs Linux when the job needs a camera, a screen or a full network stack. Local computing matters because a decision may be needed in milliseconds, the link may be down, and shipping every raw sample wastes radio energy.

sections.h3: The radio links that carry IoT data

blocks.text: A radio link is chosen on three numbers: range, data rate and energy per bit. No standard is best on all three, so IoT uses a family of them.

items: IEEE 802.15.4: 2.4 GHz, up to 250 kbit/s, short range, years on two AA cells. It defines only the physical and MAC layers.
ZigBee adds a mesh network layer and application profiles on top of 802.15.4; used in smart meters and home lighting.
Bluetooth Classic carries a continuous stream such as a headset. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) sends small bursts and runs a year on a coin cell — fitness bands, shop beacons.
Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) gives megabits per second but draws too much current for a battery node, so it suits mains-powered devices.
LoRaWAN: unlicensed sub-GHz band, a few kilometres in a city, a few kbit/s, years of battery life.

NB-IoT: narrowband radio inside licensed cellular spectrum, run by the mobile operator. Built for massive numbers of low-throughput devices, long battery life, deep coverage into basements, and low device cost. It needs a SIM and a data plan.

Mobile internet: LTE is the 4G packet-data standard from 3GPP that made cellular data cheap enough for machines. 5G adds three service classes — enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB, fast downloads), massive machine-type communication (mMTC, very many low-rate devices) and ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC, factory control).

blocks.text: Protocol stacks and frame formats are in Unit 3.

sections.h3: Cloud, big data, edge and fog

blocks.text: Cloud computing rents compute and storage by the hour. A device usually never contacts a database directly; it publishes to a broker, and the cloud platform authenticates the device, stores the readings and serves them to phone apps. See Unit 5.

Big data analytics handles streams too large or too fast for one machine. Stream processing keeps a moving average over the last ten minutes; batch processing runs a nightly report over months of history.

Edge computing moves computation to the gateway or to the device itself, and fog computing is the older name for the same idea placed at intermediate nodes between device and cloud. Three reasons: latency, bandwidth cost, and continued operation when the link drops — a Chennai flat keeps its last reading on the local gateway during a power cut and uploads when the network returns.

blocks.where: D is bytes uploaded per day; N is the number of devices; S is bytes per sample; T is seconds between two samples from one device; 86,400 is the number of seconds in a day.

figure.caption: The worked example run end to end: a sensor sends one 512-byte sample every 30 minutes, and 10,000 such devices together upload 245.76 MB per day. The shaded final box is the fleet total that the exam asks for.

spec.title: Worked example 1: uplink per day
spec.aria: A downward four-step flow: 10,000 sensors each sending 512 bytes every 30 minutes give 48 samples per day, then 24,576 bytes per device per day, then 245,760,000 bytes for all devices, and finally 245.76 MB uploaded per day.

examples.question: A narrowband sensor sends one sample of 512 bytes every 30 minutes. There are 10,000 such devices. Find the total uplink data per day in MB, taking 1 MB = 10^6 bytes.
steps: Samples per device per day = 24 × 60 ÷ 30 = 48 samples.
Bytes per device per day = 512 bytes × 48 = 24,576 bytes.
Convert to MB: 245,760,000 ÷ 10^6 = 245.76 MB per day.
examples.answer: The 10,000 devices upload 245.76 MB per day in total.
examples.check:
n = 10000
s = 512
t = 30 * 60
per_day = (24 * 3600) // t
b = s * per_day
total = n * b
mb = total / 1e6
print(per_day)
print(b)
print(total)
print(mb)

traps: NB-IoT is not fast 5G. A question about video, megabits per second or millisecond latency is not an NB-IoT question — NB-IoT is for very many slow devices with years of battery life.
IEEE 802.15.4 and ZigBee are not the same standard. 802.15.4 covers the physical and MAC layers only; ZigBee adds network and application layers on top.
1 MB means 10^6 bytes in these sums. If the question says MiB, divide by 2^20 = 1,048,576 instead, and the answer changes.
RFID identifies a thing; a sensor measures a quantity. Writing that an RFID tag “senses temperature” loses the mark.
LoRaWAN works in unlicensed spectrum with no SIM; NB-IoT needs licensed spectrum, an operator, a SIM and a data plan. The examiner checks which constraint you noticed.

quiz.q: Name four families of IoT enabling technologies.
quiz.a: Sensing and identification (sensors, RFID); embedded computing (microcontrollers, single-board computers); wireless links (IEEE 802.15.4, ZigBee, BLE, Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, 4G/5G); cloud, big data analytics, and edge or fog computing.
Enhanced mobile broadband, massive machine-type communication, ultra-reliable low-latency communication — the three 5G service classes.

quiz.q: Why does a node in a wireless sensor network forward another node's packets?
quiz.a: Radio range is short and nodes are dense, so a gateway may be several hops away. Forwarding lets data reach it, and many short hops cost less transmit energy per node than one long, unreliable hop.

quiz.q: Cloud computing already exists. Why add edge computing?
quiz.a: Three reasons: latency, since a local decision can be made in milliseconds; bandwidth cost, since sending summaries instead of raw samples is cheaper; and availability, since the gateway keeps working when the uplink drops.

quiz.q: 2000 devices each send 256 bytes every 15 minutes. Find the total uplink per day in MB, with 1 MB = 10^6 bytes.
quiz.a: Samples per device per day = 24 × 60 ÷ 15 = 96. Bytes per device = 256 × 96 = 24,576. Total = 2000 × 24,576 = 49,152,000 bytes = 49.152 MB per day.

quiz.q: A city must read 5000 water meters placed in basements, once an hour, for ten years on one battery per meter. Choose between ZigBee and NB-IoT and justify.
quiz.a: NB-IoT. Basements need deep indoor coverage, which licensed cellular spectrum gives; the meters are low-throughput (a hundred bytes an hour is trivial) and need years of battery life, which is exactly NB-IoT's design point. ZigBee needs a mains-powered gateway within short range and a mesh that may not reach a basement, and it shifts maintenance to the city. The cost is a SIM and a data plan per meter.

quiz.q: A factory arm must stop within 5 ms of a fault signal, and a security camera streams 4K video. Which 5G service class fits each, and why not the third?
quiz.a: The arm uses URLLC, which guarantees low latency and high reliability. The camera uses eMBB, which gives high throughput. mMTC fits neither, because it trades rate and latency for supporting a very large number of low-rate devices.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry these technologies are chosen as one chain — sensor, radio, network, platform — and the radio is picked only after the range, rate and battery budget are known. Newer research adds ambient backscatter, tags that reflect existing signals instead of generating their own; ambient IoT, being standardised for 5G-Advanced; and satellite non-terrestrial networks for areas no tower reaches. Protocol-level detail for all of these is in Unit 3. Useful search terms: 3GPP LPWA, 802.11ah Wi-Fi HaLow, ambient IoT.
